subject: Archaeology
title: The Thames Foreshore
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Thames Foreshore.

hook.text: When the tide drops, 2,000 years of London appear — Roman shoes and Tudor pins.

buildup.text: Mudlarkers walk the riverbank daily, finding objects washed from eroding banks.

discovery.text: One session yielded a pilgrim badge, a Roman lamp, and a 500-year-old shoe.

twist.text: Climate-driven tidal erosion frees more artifacts but sweeps many out to sea.

climax.text: The Museum of London displays thousands of foreshore finds from citizen mudlarkers.

punchline.text: The Thames is London's longest museum. Every low tide opens it.

quiz.question: How is climate change affecting Thames foreshore archaeology?
options: Warmer water dissolves metal artifacts before they can be found
Increased erosion frees more artifacts but sweeps them out to sea
Higher temperatures attract invasive species that damage finds

details.summary: The Thames foreshore in London is a living archaeological site exposed twice daily by tides. Mudlarkers and archaeologists find Roman coins, medieval pilgrim badges, Tudor clay pipes, and Victorian artifacts — a continuous 2,000-year record of London's history washed by every tide cycle.
details.whyItMatters: The Thames foreshore makes archaeology accessible to everyone. It demonstrates that significant archaeological sites exist in unexpected urban contexts and that ordinary objects tell extraordinary stories about daily life through the centuries.
takeaways: The Thames foreshore exposes ancient artifacts with each tide
Finds span 2,000 years from Roman to Victorian periods
Mudlarking makes urban archaeology accessible to the public

faq.question: What kinds of artifacts are found on the Thames foreshore?
faq.answer: Roman coins, medieval pottery, Tudor-era clay pipes, Georgian buttons, Victorian bottles, and objects from every period of London's history. The anaerobic mud preserves organic materials like leather shoes and wooden objects that would decay in dry soil. Each tide reveals new finds.

faq.question: Is mudlarking on the Thames legal?
faq.answer: A free permit from the Port of London Authority allows surface finds. Digging below the foreshore surface requires an additional permit. Significant finds must be reported to the Portable Antiquities Scheme. The system balances public access with heritage protection.
